### **4.3.6 Littoral Forest**

Littoral forest is a common vegetation type occurring on tropical shores.

--- SENTENCE 1003 ---
It often consists of a dense forest dominated by a single tree species.

--- SENTENCE 1004 ---
The major factor determining the distribution and extent of littoral forests is the ocean.

--- SENTENCE 1005 ---
Common characteristics for tree species in the community include tolerance of bright sunny conditions, dispersal by buoyant, salt-tolerant seeds (or hitchhiking on seabirds), and tolerance to salt spray and wind.

--- SENTENCE 1006 ---
However, most species are not tolerant of standing water or frequent incursions of saltwater (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1007 ---
Typically, the forest floor is open due to the lack of bright sunlight required for germination and growth of most herbs and shrubs on the beach strand (Whistler 1992).

--- SENTENCE 1008 ---
The limiting factor for tree species is substrate and soils (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1009 ---
The dominant tree species of Samoa include: *Barringtonia asiatica* and *Calophyllum inophyllum* in certain beach areas and historically pu'a vai on Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1010 ---
But other tree species that may also thrive in this forest type include *Hernandia nymphaeifolia*, *Terminalia catappa*, *Cordia subcordata*, *Neisosperma oppositifolium*, *Guettarda speciosa*, *Thespesia populnea*, *Tournefortia argentea*, and *Cocos nucifera*.

--- SENTENCE 1011 ---
Although common and sometimes dominant on Polynesian shores, coconut trees have presumably been planted or are remnants of former cultivation due to their presence mostly in or near villages and coastal plantations.

--- SENTENCE 1012 ---
A map made in 1839 shows Rose Island extended across the width of the atoll rim and was covered by forests (Keating 1992).

--- SENTENCE 1013 ---
When Alfred Goldsborough Mayor did the first scientific account of Rose Atoll in 1920, he found the southern and southeastern half of Rose Island covered with a dense pu'a vai-dominated forest, with no other understory plants, except a single coconut tree.

--- SENTENCE 1014 ---
The largest trees were found near the southern end of the forest.

--- SENTENCE 1015 ---
Plant observations from 1974 to 1988 have documented at least 10 additional species that were established at one point (Wegmann and Holzwarth 2006).

--- SENTENCE 1016 ---
However, during the visit in 2010, eight species (*Boerhavia repens*, *Tournefortia argentea*, *Pisonia grandis*, *Portulaca lutea*, *Hibiscus tiliaceus*, *Nephrolepis hirsutula*, *Cocos nucifera*, *Cordia subcordata*) were documented.

--- SENTENCE 1017 ---
Appendix A lists the plant species of Rose Atoll, collections or first observations, and most recent information about current presence or absence.

--- SENTENCE 1018 ---
Rose Atoll's littoral forest is currently dominated by *Tournefortia argentea* which forms a forest up to 25 feet tall.

--- SENTENCE 1019 ---
Historically Rose Island supported a mature stand of pu'a vai.

!

--- SENTENCE 1020 ---
*Left photo: Rose Island from the sea in 1939, dominated by pu'a vai.*

--- SENTENCE 1021 ---
Right photo: Rose Island from the lagoon in 2007 with just a few unhealthy trees remaining.

--- SENTENCE 1022 ---
* USFWS

Pu'a vai *(Pisonia grandis)*, found almost exclusively in Indo-Pacific islands from tropical Africa to eastern Polynesia and Micronesia, is spread by sticky fruits that become attached to seabirds.

--- SENTENCE 1023 ---
It is a shade-intolerant plant that thrives on sandy shores and islands, particularly in soil enriched with guano from seabirds.

--- SENTENCE 1024 ---
The distinct soil in the *Pu'a vai*grove on Rose Island consists of an upper layer of rich chocolate-colored humus, which extends to over 6 feet in depth (Mayor 1921, Lipman and Taylor 1924) overlying the calcium carbonate bedrock.

--- SENTENCE 1025 ---
*Pu'a vai* is considered "one of the most salttolerant plants of which we have record at present" that is able to inhabit the unusually high salt concentrations in the soil on Rose Island (Lipman and Shelley 1924).

--- SENTENCE 1026 ---
The lack of fresh surface water and the properties of the soil most likely explain the limited number of plant species that are on the atoll (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1027 ---
*Pisonia* forests are declining throughout the Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 1028 ---
Historically, the best example of a *Pisonia* forest in American Samoa, Rose Island's *Pisonia* forest has undergone several gradual periods of dieback and regeneration.

--- SENTENCE 1029 ---
The dieback was noted in the early 1970s but the forest was regenerating by 1976 (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1030 ---
The cause of this dieback was unknown, but thought to be disease, drought, or an insect attack (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1031 ---
First documented in 2002, the soft scale insect (*Pulvinaria urbicola*) is associated with the once healthy forest's decline (Wegmann and Holzwarth 2006).

--- SENTENCE 1032 ---
*Scale insect on* Pisonia *leaf.

--- SENTENCE 1033 ---
Kelsie Ernsberger/USFWS

May 2004, 10 of the remaining 11 mature *Pisonia* trees were treated with injections of a systemic pesticide called imidacloprid (Trade name Imicide ®).

--- SENTENCE 1034 ---
Loss of trees continued so it appears the response may have come too late and this approach alone has not significantly deterred the scale infestation.

--- SENTENCE 1035 ---
Scale insect infestation is associated with significant loss of *Pisonia* forests worldwide (Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service 2006, 2007).

--- SENTENCE 1036 ---
Additionally, since the Polynesian rat was eradicated in 1993 coconut palms have been released from rat herbivory and have increased to a population size that threatens to shade out recruitment of native canopy trees.

--- SENTENCE 1037 ---
The *Pisonia* trees along with tree heliotrope serve as important nesting and roosting habitat for the red-footed booby, great and lesser frigatebird, gogo uli , and white tern, which prefer to nest above the ground on trees.

--- SENTENCE 1038 ---
Tree heliotrope also provides cover for red-tailed tropicbirds, brown noddies, sooty terns, and brown boobies, which nest directly on the ground.

--- SENTENCE 1039 ---
Shrubs and rock piles also provide shade and daytime cover for the numerous land hermit crabs that inhabit the island.

--- SENTENCE 1040 ---
Thick vegetation and rock crevices also provide shelter and protection for the largest land crab, the coconut crab (*Birgus latro*).

--- SENTENCE 1041 ---
This species seems to have increased in density since the eradication of rats at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1042 ---
The relatively open understory of the *Pisonia* forest is also favored habitat for Pacific goldenplovers, wandering tattlers, and ruddy turnstones (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1043 ---
Littoral forests were at one time a common habitat in the Pacific; however, human alteration of island landscapes has limited this forest type.

--- SENTENCE 1044 ---
The eradication of rats from Rose Atoll by 1993 provides important habitat for plant species that will be able to recolonize the atoll and perpetuate the littoral habitats that are in decline throughout the Pacific region.

--- SENTENCE 1045 ---
*4.4 Threatened, Endangered, and Sensitive Species**

One goal of the Refuge System is "to conserve, restore where appropriate, and enhance all species of fish, wildlife, and plants that are endangered or threatened with becoming endangered."

--- SENTENCE 1046 ---
In the policy clarifying the mission of the Refuge System, it is stated, "we protect and manage candidate and proposed species to enhance their status and help preclude the need for listing."

--- SENTENCE 1047 ---
In accordance with this policy, the CCP planning team considered species with Federal or State/Territory status, and other special status species, in the planning process.

--- SENTENCE 1048 ---
## **4.4.1 Tuli'olovalu (***Numenius tahitiensis***) or Bristle-thighed Curlew**

Tuli'olovalu breed in western Alaska and migrate during the winter to remote, small islands and atolls in the tropical Pacific Ocean (Marks and Redmond 1994).

--- SENTENCE 1049 ---
The beaches and littoral forest of the atoll are important wintering ground for tuli'olovalu .

--- SENTENCE 1050 ---
This rare shorebird is the only migratory species whose entire population is restricted to the insular Pacific (Hayman et al.

--- SENTENCE 1051 ---
1986, Marks et al. 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1052 ---
Marks and Redmond (1996) documented the strong fidelity shown by tuli to wintering sites.

--- SENTENCE 1053 ---
At Laysan Island in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (NWHI), only 1 of 16 marked adult tuli'olovalu changed its wintering home range area in 3 years of study (Marks and Redmond 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1054 ---
This species undergoes a molt-induced flightless period (unique in shorebirds) and leaves many birds more susceptible to predatory attacks during that time (Marks 1993, Marks and Redmond 1994).

--- SENTENCE 1055 ---
Therefore, predator-free islands to which these birds are adapted have become increasingly important as competition for space increases and less habitat is available due to an increasing human population.

--- SENTENCE 1056 ---
With a global population of approximately 10,000 individuals (Morrison et al. 2006), the Service (USFWS 2008) has designated the curlew as a Bird of Conservation Concern and it is also ranked as Vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)

--- SENTENCE 1057 ---
(Engilis and Naughton 2004, IUCN 2008).

--- SENTENCE 1058 ---
It is also highlighted as a globally threatened species in need of regional action by the South Pacific Regional Environmental Programme.

### **4.4.2 Tuli (***Pluvialis fulva***) or Pacific Golden Plover**

The Pacific golden plover breeds in western Alaska and Siberia and winters throughout the Pacific Islands.

--- SENTENCE 1059 ---
Plovers foraging at Rose Atoll likely come from the Alaskan breeding population, however, these affinities are still poorly understood (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1060 ---
Tuli are widespread across the Pacific region in any open habitat from beach strands to upland pastures, occurring in good numbers on remote islands and atolls.

--- SENTENCE 1061 ---
Amerson et al. (1982) estimated 4,500 tuli in American Samoa, a small population number relative to the total United States Pacific Islands (USPI) populations (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1062 ---
Johnson et al. (2008) studied migration behavior of Pacific golden plover in American Samoa and were able to confirm that at least 1 of the 30 birds they tagged on Tutuila Island was breeding in Alaska.

--- SENTENCE 1063 ---
The birds departed Samoa for the northward migration in mid-April.

--- SENTENCE 1064 ---
The return of the plovers began in late August and peaked in mid-September.

--- SENTENCE 1065 ---
This represents at least a 5,594-mile trip from American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 1066 ---
Johnson et al. (2008) estimated there were 500 tuli on Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 1067 ---
The largest count of tuli recorded at Rose Atoll was 49 individuals in 1984.

--- SENTENCE 1068 ---
The USPI Regional Shorebird Conservation Plan identified the Pacific Golden Plover as a species of High Conservation Concern (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

### **4.4.3 I'a sa (***Chelonia mydas***) or Green Turtle**

I'a sa is listed as threatened under the ESA.

--- SENTENCE 1069 ---
Adults can weigh up to 500 pounds and are often found living near tropical reefs and rocky shorelines.

--- SENTENCE 1070 ---
Females may lay up to 6 clutches per season in pits excavated in soft beach sand, with each clutch containing about 100 eggs.

--- SENTENCE 1071 ---
Hatchlings and juveniles live in pelagic waters.

--- SENTENCE 1072 ---
Little information exists on the feeding behavior of post-hatchlings and juveniles living in pelagic habitats, but most likely they are exclusively carnivorous (e.g., soft-bodied invertebrates, jellyfish, and fish eggs).

--- SENTENCE 1073 ---
Subadult and adult turtles residing in nearshore benthic environments are almost completely herbivorous; their common name is derived from the color of the animals' body fat, which is green from the marine algae and sea grasses they eat.

!

--- SENTENCE 1074 ---
*I'a sa swimming in Rose Atoll lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 1075 ---
Kelsie Ernsberger/USFWS

I'a sa use the protected habitats of Rose Atoll for feeding and nesting.

--- SENTENCE 1076 ---
Their numbers have declined throughout the south Pacific due to the combined effects of habitat destruction, human harvest for meat and shells, depredation by introduced predators, and incidental drowning in fishing gear (Kinan 2005, Craig 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1077 ---
The isolated beaches on Rose Atoll provide an important nesting ground for i'a sa.

--- SENTENCE 1078 ---
The number of i'a sa nesting annually at Rose Atoll has been estimated at 24–36 (Tuato'o-Bartley et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1079 ---
However, the total number of i'a sa using Rose Atoll as a nesting ground could actually be several fold higher, since females only nest every 2–5 years (Spotila 2004, NMFS and USFWS

1998a), and thus a different set of turtles nest each season.

--- SENTENCE 1080 ---
Given the scarcity of beaches where turtles can nest and their eggs hatch unmolested, the value of the isolated beaches at Rose Atoll is considerable, even if only 120 or so i'a sa nest there.

--- SENTENCE 1081 ---
The Historical Summary of Turtle Observations at Rose Atoll, American Samoa, 1839–1991 (Balazs 1991) is a compilation of historical data and notations.

--- SENTENCE 1082 ---
The document lists a total of 47 entries for that time period, most of the earlier ones simply report presence or absence of turtles.

--- SENTENCE 1083 ---
From 1970

onward, turtle observations were more quantitative, if no less sporadic and opportunistic due to the expense of reaching the remote atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1084 ---
Aerial, land-based, and water-based surveys recorded the number of turtles, their tracks, nest pits, eggs, hatchlings, and nesting and mating behaviors (Balazs 1991).

--- SENTENCE 1085 ---
An estimated 200 turtles were seen in the lagoon during an aerial survey in August 1974, the highest value recorded.

--- SENTENCE 1086 ---
A total of 406 pits were counted on both Rose and Sand Islands during a survey in October 1976.

--- SENTENCE 1087 ---
A decade later, in fall 1985, biologists counted a total of 244 pits on both islands, and a decade after that, in fall 1992, the total count was 81 nesting pits.

--- SENTENCE 1088 ---
However, the problem with nest pit counts is that female turtles often dig test pits before actually laying eggs, and they lay multiple clutches the year they make the long migration to their natal nesting beach.

--- SENTENCE 1089 ---
Also, unless there is a major storm event that wipes the beach clean, it is difficult to reliably discern if a pit was dug that season or the season before (Ponwith 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1090 ---
These limitations, as well as uneven survey effort, should be taken into account when comparing pit counts from various years, and it should be recognized that pit counts are not the equivalent of a population count.

--- SENTENCE 1091 ---
The i'a sa that visit Rose do so seasonally for reproduction, and spend the rest of their time in other parts of the south Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 1092 ---
Metal flipper tags were applied to a total of 46 nesting females from 1971 to 1996 in order to see where they traveled (Balazs 1991).

--- SENTENCE 1093 ---
Three of these tags were re-sighted after the turtles were killed for food or fatally injured from a hunting attempt.

--- SENTENCE 1094 ---
Two were located in Fiji at the time of tag recovery and one in Vanuatu (both island groups to the west of Samoa).

--- SENTENCE 1095 ---
A fourth turtle was re-sighted at Rose Atoll, 9 years after she was initially tagged (Ponwith 1990), making multiple visits to the beach to nest.

--- SENTENCE 1096 ---
Given the limited re-sighting rate of flipper tags, satellite tagging was subsequently employed in an effort to better comprehend the migration routes of green turtles in the south Pacific (Craig et al. 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1097 ---
Seven females at Rose Atoll were outfitted with satellite tags during the nesting seasons of 1993 to 1995.

--- SENTENCE 1098 ---
After 2 months of nesting at Rose, six of the turtles traveled to feeding grounds in Fiji.

--- SENTENCE 1099 ---
The seventh turtle traveled due east to Raiatea, an island in French Polynesia.

--- SENTENCE 1100 ---
The turtles' migration route crossed 994 miles of ocean and took an average of 40 days.

--- SENTENCE 1101 ---
The route followed prevailing surface currents as recorded by satellite-linked ocean drifters deployed from Rose in February 2002, though the drifters traveled more slowly (net rate of 1.0 foot per hour) than the turtles (3.6 feet per hour).

--- SENTENCE 1102 ---
While these i'a sa spend the majority of their life in Fiji, accumulating the fat stores that will enable them to reproduce, the remote beaches at Rose Atoll provide invaluable undisturbed nesting habitat (Craig et al. 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1103 ---
Unlike many places in their range, at Rose Atoll, turtles can approach the beach without risk of being harvested for meat or drowned in nets, and eggs and hatchlings are free from depredation by wild pigs, rats, dogs, and humans.

--- SENTENCE 1104 ---
Marine debris can also prove deadly when it entangles turtles or is mistaken for food and ingested.

--- SENTENCE 1105 ---
Plastics are particularly harmful as they may remain in the turtle's stomach for long periods of time, releasing toxic substances, and can clog the digestive system.

--- SENTENCE 1106 ---
Natural predators and dangers inherent to the human populated areas east of Samoa where the turtles feed continue to impact turtle populations.

--- SENTENCE 1107 ---
Craig et al. (2004) stresses the importance of working towards protection for turtles in their foraging waters east of Samoa, since this is where turtles spend 90% of their adult life.

--- SENTENCE 1108 ---
Continued monitoring of the nesting beaches at Rose Atoll will give researchers a proxy for population trends of i'a sa in the region.

--- SENTENCE 1109 ---
# **4.4.4 Hawksbill Turtle (***Eretmochelys imbricata***)**

Hawksbill turtles use the protected habitats of Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1110 ---
Similar to i'a sa, their numbers have declined throughout the south Pacific, reduced by the combined effects of habitat destruction, human harvest for meat and tortoise shell, depredation by introduced predators, and incidental drowning in fishing gear (Kinan 2005; Craig 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1111 ---
Although it is not clear if hawksbills nest at Rose Atoll, they are consistently sighted using the lagoon and open water habitats around the atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1112 ---
The hawksbill turtle is listed as endangered under the ESA.

--- SENTENCE 1113 ---
It is one of the smaller turtles and takes its species name (*imbricata*) from the overlapping plates on its upper shell and its common name from the shape of its hooked jaw.

--- SENTENCE 1114 ---
The carapace (top shell) of an adult ranges from 25-35 inches in length and has a "tortoiseshell" coloring, ranging from dark to golden brown, with streaks of orange, red, and/or black.

--- SENTENCE 1115 ---
Hawksbill turtles use different habitats at different stages of their life cycle, but are typically found around coastal reefs, rocky areas, estuaries, and lagoons.

--- SENTENCE 1116 ---
Their narrow head and jaws, shaped like a beak, allow them to get food from crevices in tropical reefs.

--- SENTENCE 1117 ---
They eat sponges, anemones, squid, and shrimp.

--- SENTENCE 1118 ---
Hawksbills have been consistently reported at Rose Atoll in historical accounts (Setchell 1924), as well as more recent surveys (Sekora 1974, Ludwig 1981, Amerson et al. 1982, Morrell et al. 1991, Flint 1992, NMFS PIFSC 2006).

### **4.4.5 Faisua (***Tridacna maxima***) or Giant Clam**

The colloquial term "giant clam" refers to eight species of marine bivalves found in two genera (*Hippopus* and *Tridacna*) of the molluscan subfamily Tridacninae.

--- SENTENCE 1119 ---
Surveys of faisua populations at Rose Atoll have identified a single species, *Tridacna maxima* (Wass 1981, Green and Craig 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1120 ---
Less than a third of the size of the "true" giant clam *Tridacna gigas*, *T. maxima* is commonly referred to as the "small giant clam," with shells generally not exceeding 9 inches in length.

--- SENTENCE 1121 ---
Found living on the surface of reefs or sand, or partly embedded in coral, the faisua occupies well-lit areas, due to the symbiotic relationship with single-celled photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) found in its fleshy mantle that require sunlight for energy production.

--- SENTENCE 1122 ---
Faisua also filter-feed on phytoplankton extracted from seawater siphoned through their body.

--- SENTENCE 1123 ---
Mature faisua are hermaphrodites that reproduce by broadcast spawning, releasing sperm first, followed by eggs.

--- SENTENCE 1124 ---
The fertilized egg develops into a larva within 3 hours and passes through two additional larval stages before undergoing metamorphosis after 8-10 days into a juvenile, sessile

faisua that acquires zooxanthellae.

--- SENTENCE 1125 ---
Reproductive and growth studies at Rose Atoll (Radtke 1985) showed the clams reach maturity at about 10 years of age corresponding to a shell size of 3–5 inches.

--- SENTENCE 1126 ---
Young faisua are male and put most of their energy into growth, becoming hermaphrodites upon maturity and accompanied by a slower growth phase.

--- SENTENCE 1127 ---
Reproduction is stimulated by the lunar cycle, the time of day, and the presence of others eggs and sperm in the water.

--- SENTENCE 1128 ---
Faisua lifespan at Rose Atoll is estimated to be approximately 28 years.

--- SENTENCE 1129 ---
*Tridacna maxima* has the widest geographic range of all giant clam species.

--- SENTENCE 1130 ---
It is found in the oceans surrounding east Africa, India, China,

!

--- SENTENCE 1131 ---
*Faisua (*Tridacna maxima*) embedded in* Astreopora *coral.*

--- SENTENCE 1132 ---
Kelsie Ernsberger/USFWS

Australia, Southeast Asia, and the islands of the Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 1133 ---
Although classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, this culturally and ecologically important marine animal has declined precipitously from overharvesting in many populated areas including the high islands of American Samoa, but

remains abundant at Rose Atoll (Green and Craig 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1134 ---
*Tridacna maxima* is listed under Appendix II of CITES meaning it is not necessarily threatened but that trade must be controlled in order to avoid use incompatible with its survival.

--- SENTENCE 1135 ---
The first survey of faisua at Rose was undertaken by the American Samoa DMWR in an attempt to quantify the resource in response to requests by the Samoans that they be allowed to harvest the clams (Wass 1981).

--- SENTENCE 1136 ---
The study found faisua to be uncommon in the ava and fore reef but abundant in the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 1137 ---
Distribution in the lagoon was patchy, with faisua abundant on solid substrate in the shallow, relatively clear parts of the lagoon, but with lower densities in the southern lagoon and below approximately 45 feet where water became more turbid.

--- SENTENCE 1138 ---
Constraints of time as well as the uneven distribution of suitable clam substrate in the lagoon made density determinations difficult, with the single transect survey in the southwestern lagoon yielding an average density of 0.33 clams per square yard.

--- SENTENCE 1139 ---
Size frequency data were collected at four lagoon locations; shell measurements ranged from 0.4 to 9 inches, with approximately 31% being greater than 5.5 inches, the size at which all clams are fully hermaphroditic.

--- SENTENCE 1140 ---
More extensive transects by Radtke (1985) in various habitats showed marked differences related to depth and substrate.

--- SENTENCE 1141 ---
Lagoon patch reefs in 20–40 feet of water were concluded to be prime habitat for faisua, with densities of 3.6–7.2 clams per square yard and 40–50% of the area colonized.

--- SENTENCE 1142 ---
Smaller coral patches (with up to 3.6 clams per square yard) and lagoon substrate (with up to 6 clams per square yard) were colonized at approximately 20%.

--- SENTENCE 1143 ---
Shell measurement ranged from 0.4 to 9 inches, with bimodal peaks around 1–2 inches and 6–7 inches.

--- SENTENCE 1144 ---
Radtke's total estimated number of faisua in the lagoon was approximately 1,338,000.

--- SENTENCE 1145 ---
Unlike Wass (1981) Radtke did not favor controlled harvesting, stating, "they have a respectable number of organisms in this ecosystem, but due to their slow growth would have a small sustainable yield … quantitative balance of production of *Tridacna maxima* at Rose Atoll does not appear to be within the scope of rational exploitation and exploitation could endanger the perpetuity of the unique environment.

--- SENTENCE 1146 ---
"

A pivotal study by Green and Craig (1999) highlights the importance of Rose Atoll as a refuge for faisua.

--- SENTENCE 1147 ---
From 1994 to 1995 they surveyed all 6 islands of American Samoa and recorded a total of 2,853 clams in survey transects, 97% of which were found at Rose.

--- SENTENCE 1148 ---
The majority were located in the lagoon, with faisua favoring areas at the base of pinnacle patch reefs.

--- SENTENCE 1149 ---
Roughly a quarter of the clams were mature in size, and mortality was estimated as being very low, due mostly to natural causes.

--- SENTENCE 1150 ---
The largest clam recorded was 11 inches across the widest part of the shell.

--- SENTENCE 1151 ---
Given the mean density of faisua, the population at Rose was estimated to be approximately 27,800 clams.

--- SENTENCE 1152 ---
The dramatically lower estimate than that provided by Radtke (1985) was considered to be the result of differences in sampling design rather than a population decline.

--- SENTENCE 1153 ---
The authors theoretically considered Rose to be a potential source of faisua recruits to other islands in the Samoan archipelago, given larval longevity (approximately 8 days, range 5–15 days) and water currents flowing westward from Rose at 16 miles per day.

--- SENTENCE 1154 ---
Towed-diver surveys conducted by NMFS PIFSC in 2006 recorded more than 1,100 giant clams on 30 linear miles of transect, with approximately 95% recorded on reefs inside the lagoon (NMFS PIFSC 2006).

--- SENTENCE 1155 ---
Researchers have noted that the pinnacle just inside the ava had a markedly lower density of faisua than the rest of the lagoon and it seems likely that this is where illegal harvesting has taken place (Wegmann and Holzwarth 2006).

--- SENTENCE 1156 ---
# **4.5 Seabirds**

Rose Atoll's importance to seabirds in the South central Pacific is disproportionately large relative to the size of its islands because some of the seabird species have been extirpated on most other islands in the region.

--- SENTENCE 1157 ---
There are very few uninhabited islands in the region so Rose provides breeding habitat for species that do not thrive in proximity to human settlements.

--- SENTENCE 1158 ---
Seabirds and migratory shorebirds are the numerically dominant terrestrial vertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 1159 ---
Since 1975, 16 species of seabirds have been recorded on land and 12 species are known to breed there.

--- SENTENCE 1160 ---
Efforts to eradicate the island of Polynesian rats began in 1991, with eradication declared in 1993.

--- SENTENCE 1161 ---
This enhanced the value of the atoll for seabird conservation and has increased the possibilities that other Pacific seabird species that are currently threatened from habitat loss, predation, and invasive species, such as ta'i'o (wedge-tailed shearwaters), Christmas shearwaters, Bulwer's petrel, Phoenix petrel, and the Polynesian storm petrel, might someday colonize the site.

--- SENTENCE 1162 ---
Social attraction methods may accelerate or facilitate this process of recruitment.

--- SENTENCE 1163 ---
Rose Atoll falls into the North American Bird Conservation Region called "Other U.S. Pacific Islands" and is now considered separately from sites in the Caribbean (USFWS 2008).

--- SENTENCE 1164 ---
For most if not all of the seabirds, listed terrestrial threats such as habitat destruction, invasive weeds, disturbance, ungulates, and introduced predators limit populations (Metz and Schreiber 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1165 ---
Introduced predators such as rats, mongooses, and cats have reduced populations at many sites worldwide (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1166 ---
Seabirds using terrestrial habitats at Rose Atoll all forage in the pelagic zone typically in association with large epipelagic subsurface predators such as skipjack (*Katsuwonus pelamis*) and yellowfin tunas (*Thunnus albacares*).

--- SENTENCE 1167 ---
These fish concentrate and force prey to the surface in the course of their own foraging and also make it available to foraging seabirds (Au and Pitman 1988).

--- SENTENCE 1168 ---
El Niño-Southern Oscillation conditions can cause total or partial breeding failure in some locations (Schreiber and Schreiber 1989, Schreiber 1994, Orta 1992b) when changes in the temperature of water masses in proximity to the breeding sites change and force tuna to move elsewhere to find their preferred thermal conditions.

--- SENTENCE 1169 ---
A reduction in the biomass of these subsurface predators may render the preferred prey of tropical pelagic seabirds unavailable or difficult for the birds to detect.

--- SENTENCE 1170 ---
The relationships between these species is complex and poorly understood but it is a reasonable probability that exploitation of populations of large epipelagic fish by fishing may also affect the breeding success and survival of seabirds at Rose Atoll by reducing opportunities for this type of feeding interaction.

--- SENTENCE 1171 ---
The trophic relationships and effects on reproductive performance in this complex system have not been well quantified.

--- SENTENCE 1172 ---
# **4.5.1 Tava'e'ula (***Phaethon rubricauda***) or Red-tailed Tropicbird**

--- SENTENCE 1173 ---
The tava'e'ula is a medium-sized bird with shining pinkish-white feathers and red tail plumes.

--- SENTENCE 1174 ---
They breed mainly on oceanic islands and coral atolls in the Indian and Pacific oceans.

--- SENTENCE 1175 ---
Breeding adults are mostly sedentary; however, they avoid land when not breeding and are among the most pelagic and solitary of seabirds (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, Harrison 1990, Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1176 ---
At sea, tava'e'ula are evenly distributed throughout their range (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, King 1970).

--- SENTENCE 1177 ---
Little is known about their movements outside the breeding season.

--- SENTENCE 1178 ---
The world population is estimated at 17,000–21,000 pairs; with an estimated 12,000–14,000 pairs in the Pacific (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, Gould et al. 1974).

--- SENTENCE 1179 ---
Small colonies exist in American

Samoa and other remote Pacific islands.

--- SENTENCE 1180 ---
The largest number of active nests observed at Rose on any particular visit was 38 in 2002.

--- SENTENCE 1181 ---
The world population seems stable in many areas and may be increasing in some areas, but there is a lack of information on past population estimates so comparisons are difficult (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1182 ---
Within the USPI, tava'e'ula populations appear stable overall.

--- SENTENCE 1183 ---
Tava'e'ula nest on the ground under vegetation in the understory and base of trees, among rocks, roots, or logs and less commonly in the cavities of cliff faces (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, Orta 1992a).

--- SENTENCE 1184 ---
At Rose, red-tailed tropicbirds choose to nest under *Tournefortia* or *Pisonia* (Morell and Aquilani 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1185 ---
Nests are scrapes that vary from a shallow depression in the sand to more elaborate structures consisting of twigs and leaves (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, Harrison 1990, Fleet 1974).

--- SENTENCE 1186 ---
Breeding occurs annually, but timing varies depending on locality (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1187 ---
First breeding usually occurs around 2–4 years (Schreiber and Schreiber 1993, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1188 ---
The oldest-living bird recorded was 23 years (Klimkiewicz and Futcher 1989).

--- SENTENCE 1189 ---
Tava'e'ula are attracted to ships, presumably because flying fish, their main prey, are scattered by ships (Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1190 ---
Previously the tava'e'ula also nested on Tutuila, however the abundance of introduced animals such as rats, cats, and dogs that attack ground-nesting birds likely led to their extirpation.

--- SENTENCE 1191 ---
Introduced ants have been recorded attacking incubating adults, chicks, and eggs at some colonies in the Pacific.

### **4.5.2 Atafa (***Fregata minor***) or Great Frigatebird**

The atafa has a pantropical distribution that overlaps with lesser frigatebirds (Orta 1992b) and breeds mainly on small remote islands, typically within regions with tradewinds in the tropical Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

--- SENTENCE 1192 ---
At sea, birds can be found any distance from land but they are most abundant within 50 miles of breeding and roosting sites (King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1193 ---
Adults, juveniles, and nonbreeders disperse widely throughout the tropical seas.

--- SENTENCE 1194 ---
The world population is estimated at 500,000-1,000,000 birds (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1195 ---
A small population of fewer than 50 pairs nests on Rose Island.

--- SENTENCE 1196 ---
They are colonial nesters, often constructing platform nests in the tops of bushes and trees.

--- SENTENCE 1197 ---
At Rose Island they nest in *Tournefortia* and *Pisonia* trees.

--- SENTENCE 1198 ---
Breeding occurs throughout the year depending on locality, with egg laying primarily in the dry season (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1199 ---
Great frigatebirds are sexually dimorphic; females tend to be 25% heavier than males (Orta 1992b) and males are almost entirely black, with varying amounts of dark metallic green and purple

feathers and a large, red gular pouch that they inflate during courtship.

--- SENTENCE 1200 ---
Females are black with a white breast patch.

--- SENTENCE 1201 ---
Atafa are seasonally monogamous; it is extremely rare for pairs to remain together for subsequent breeding attempts (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1202 ---
Females breed biannually, sometimes every 3–4 years (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1203 ---
Postfledging care, which continues for up to 18 months, is provided by females.

--- SENTENCE 1204 ---
Sexual maturity begins around 8–10 years and most birds return to the natal colony to breed (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1205 ---
Atafa usually feed in mixed-species flocks over tuna schools (Orta 1992b, King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1206 ---
Jim Maragos/USFWS

consists mostly of flying fish and squid which they capture at or above the water's surface (Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1207 ---
Frigatebirds are notorious for their kleptoparasitism (a form of feeding where one animal takes prey from another that has caught or killed it), but most of their food is obtained by fishing (Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1208 ---
Tuna fisheries exploitation likely could lead to the decrease in availability of prey for atafa (Metz and Schreiber 2002).

### **4.5.3 Atafa (***Fregata ariel***) or Lesser Frigatebird**

The lesser frigatebird is also called atafa and has a pantropical distribution that coincides with, but is smaller than, that of the great frigatebird (Orta 1992b, Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1209 ---
At sea, birds are most abundant within 50 miles of breeding and roosting islands although they can be found any distance from land (King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1210 ---
Juveniles and nonbreeders disperse throughout tropical seas (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1211 ---
The species' world population is estimated at several hundred thousand birds (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1212 ---
Small colonies exist in American Samoa (Amerson et al. 1982) with fewer than 100 pairs nesting at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1213 ---
Within the USPI, lesser frigatebird populations have significantly declined due to the introduction of cats and rats; however, eradication of cats at Howland Island and Jarvis Island NWRs seems to have resulted in an increase in lesser frigatebird populations at those sites (USFWS 2005, Rauzon et al. 2011).

--- SENTENCE 1214 ---
Human exploitation of tuna fisheries could potentially affect prey availability for lesser frigatebirds because they rely upon the large subsurface predators to push the species on which they feed to the surface (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1215 ---
Breeding takes place on small, remote tropical islands.

--- SENTENCE 1216 ---
Nests and stick platforms are constructed on trees and bushes (e.g., *Pisonia* and *Tournefortia* bushes and trees on Rose Island), but when suitable vegetation is not available birds nest on bare ground (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1217 ---
Lesser frigatebirds are sexually dimorphic; females tend to be heavier than males and males have a scarlet gular pouch that is inflated during courtship displays (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1218 ---
They are seasonally monogamous; it is unlikely that pairs remain together for future breeding attempts (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1219 ---
If successful, females can only breed successfully every 2–3 years since post-fledging care is provided by the female and can last 4–6+ months (Orta 1992b).

--- SENTENCE 1220 ---
Age to sexual maturity is unknown (Orta 1992b)

--- SENTENCE 1221 ---
but probably similar to that of great frigatebird at 8–10 years.

--- SENTENCE 1222 ---
Lesser frigatebirds feed in pelagic waters, usually in mixed-species flocks over tuna schools (Orta 1992b, King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1223 ---
Their diet consists primarily of flying fish and squid that they capture at or above the water's surface (Nelson 1976).

--- SENTENCE 1224 ---
Lesser frigatebirds are also notorious for kleptoparasitism but obtain most of their food by direct capture (Nelson 1976).

--- SENTENCE 1225 ---
# **4.5.4 Fua'o (***Sula dactylatra***) or Masked Booby**

Masked boobies have a pantropical distribution (Anderson 1993, Woodward 1972).

--- SENTENCE 1226 ---
There are four subspecies; *S. d. personata* breeds on islands in the central and western Pacific (Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1227 ---
Within the USPI, the largest colonies are on Howland, Baker, and Jarvis Islands, but a significant portion of the population nests in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

--- SENTENCE 1228 ---
Birds forage in offshore and pelagic waters (King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1229 ---
They are most abundant in the vicinity of breeding islands, but they can be encountered far out at sea (King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1230 ---
During nonbreeding periods, adults may visit sites 622– 1,243 miles from breeding colonies (Woodward 1972, Clapp and Wirtz 1975, O'Brien and Davies 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1231 ---
The world population is widely distributed and therefore difficult to estimate but is thought to be several hundred thousand birds (Anderson 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1232 ---
Within the USPI, there are approximately 8,300 breeding pairs with 1,200 pairs on Jarvis Island and over 1,500 pairs each on Howland and Baker Islands (Forsell 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1233 ---
Small colonies occur in American Samoa and Palmyra Atoll (Woodward 1972, King 1967, Anderson et al. 1982), and Wake Atoll was recently recolonized by birds banded at Johnston Atoll (Rauzon et al. 2011).

--- SENTENCE 1234 ---
Rose Atoll is home to approximately 25 pairs.

--- SENTENCE 1235 ---
Masked boobies breed on oceanic islands and atolls.

--- SENTENCE 1236 ---
They tend to nest on open ground often near a cliff edge or on low sandy beaches or rocky ground (Anderson 1993, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1237 ---
At Rose Atoll, they nest in open areas on the ground.

--- SENTENCE 1238 ---
They also form "clubs" or aggregations of nonbreeding birds on the fringe of breeding colonies (Woodward 1972).

--- SENTENCE 1239 ---
Breeding is fairly synchronous but timing varies depending on locality (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1240 ---
Masked boobies are seasonally monogamous and at least 45% of pairs at Kure Atoll retained their mates through a second breeding season (Kepler 1969).

--- SENTENCE 1241 ---
Two eggs are laid but broods are typically reduced to one chick by siblicide (Anderson 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1242 ---
Sexual maturity begins around 3–4 years and most birds return to their natal colony to breed (Anderson 1993, Nelson 1978, Kepler 1969).

--- SENTENCE 1243 ---
Adults sometimes skip a year between breeding attempts (Woodward 1972, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1244 ---
Masked boobies feed by plunge-diving and can be found more than 93 miles from land (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1245 ---
They forage singly or in mixed-species flocks associated with schooling tuna (King 1967, Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1246 ---
In Hawai'i, fish constituted greater than 97% of the diet and squid less than

Masked boobies breed on a few islands with human populations but they are vulnerable to human disturbance (Anderson 1993).

# **4.5.5 Fua'o (***Sula leucogaster***) or Brown Booby**

Fua'o have a pantropical distribution (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1255 ---
There are four subspecies; *S. l. plotus* breeds on islands in the central and western Pacific (Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1256 ---
In the USPI, brown boobies occur in the greatest numbers in the Hawaiian Islands.

--- SENTENCE 1257 ---
Breeding adults are mostly sedentary and juveniles disperse throughout the tropical seas (Carboneras 1992, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1258 ---
At sea, they occur more nearshore than the other booby species (*Sula dactylatra*) and they are rarely seen over 50 miles from the nearest land (King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1259 ---
Little is known of movements during nonbreeding periods but adults have been found up to 1,802 miles from breeding sites (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1260 ---
Worldwide, the number of brown boobies is estimated at 221,000–275,000 pairs, which includes 50,000–70,000 pairs of *S. l. plotus*

--- SENTENCE 1261 ---
(Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1262 ---
About 3,700 pairs nest in the USPI; approximately 700 nest in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 1263 ---
At Rose there are approximately 375 breeding pairs of

brown boobies.

--- SENTENCE 1264 ---
The world population has declined dramatically over the past 200 years and possibly only 1–10% of historic populations remain (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1265 ---
Currently the USPI population appears stable, with populations on Wake Atoll and Howland and Baker Islands gradually rebounding following eradication or control of cats (Rauzon et al. 2011).

--- SENTENCE 1266 ---
Fua'o breeding range overlaps with that of the other two species of booby on oceanic islands and atolls (Carboneras 1992, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1267 ---
Nesting occurs on flat ground, often on cliff ledges, but they will also nest on sandy islands and bare coral atolls (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1268 ---
At Rose Atoll, brown boobies nest on the ground under the canopy of *Pisonia* and *Tournefortia* trees.

--- SENTENCE 1269 ---
Nests vary from a scrape in the sand to a fairly well-formed pile of twigs and grasses.

--- SENTENCE 1270 ---
Breeding is synchronous but timing varies depending on locality and occurs throughout the year (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1271 ---
Brown boobies are monogamous but maintenance of long-term pair bonds varies by location (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1272 ---
Pairs lay two (vary rarely three) eggs

--- SENTENCE 1273 ---
but the brood is often reduced to one chick as a result of siblicide (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1274 ---
Age of first breeding is typically 4–5 years (Schreiber and Norton 2002, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1275 ---
Fua'o feed by plunge-diving and feeding is often solitary, but they may be found in feeding flocks with other species (Schreiber and Norton 2002, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1276 ---
They forage in nearshore waters, ranging from 5 to 44 miles from land, and feed mostly on flying fish, squid, mackerel scad, juvenile goatfish, and anchovy (Harrison 1990, Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1277 ---
The oldest-known bird was 26 years, but they probably live to at least 30 years (Schreiber and Norton 2002, Simmons 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1278 ---
Adult

survivorship was 93.2% at Kure Atoll (Tershey 1998).

--- SENTENCE 1279 ---
At Johnston Atoll, survival from fledging to breeding ranged from 30 to 40% in an 18-year study (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1280 ---
A major threat to fua'o has been the loss of habitat to development and human disturbance; newer pairs are especially vulnerable at the beginning of the breeding season (Schreiber and Norton 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1281 ---
In American Samoa, hunting pressure on brown boobies was high during historic times and this may still occur on occasion (Amerson et al. 1982).

# **4.5.6 Fua'o (***Sula sula***) or Red-footed Booby**

Red-footed boobies have a pantropical distribution that overlaps other booby species (*S. dactylatra* and *S. leucogaster*)

--- SENTENCE 1284 ---
(Schreiber et al. 1996, Carboneras 1992).

--- SENTENCE 1285 ---
There are three subspecies; *S. s. rubripes* breeds in the central and western Pacific (Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1286 ---
Red-footed boobies nest throughout the USPI.

--- SENTENCE 1287 ---
Distribution is pelagic; feeding flocks occur hundreds of miles from land (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1288 ---
Breeding adults are mostly sedentary but juveniles roost near colonies on islands other than their natal island (Schreiber et al. 1996, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1289 ---
Little is known about adult movements outside of the nesting season (Schreiber et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1290 ---
The world population was estimated at less than 300,000 pairs in 1996 (Schreiber et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1291 ---
In the USPI, there are approximately 19,000 pairs.

--- SENTENCE 1292 ---
Approximately 2,000 pairs nest in American Samoa

(Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1293 ---
Rose Atoll hosts 700 pairs of this species.

--- SENTENCE 1294 ---
The world population has been severely reduced over the last two centuries (Schreiber et al. 1996) and few data exist on current numbers (Cao et al. 2005).

--- SENTENCE 1295 ---
Cao et al. (2005) suggest the present day population size has declined to 10% of their historical values.

--- SENTENCE 1296 ---
This species of booby is the smallest of the booby species and breeds on oceanic islands and atolls (Schreiber et al. 1996, Carboneras 1992).

--- SENTENCE 1297 ---
Unlike the masked and brown boobies, these boobies roost and nest on shrubs and trees but will use bare ground or low piles of vegetation (Schreiber et al. 1996, Carboneras 1992, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1298 ---
On Rose Island, red-footed boobies build nests in *Tournefortia* and *Pisonia* trees.

--- SENTENCE 1299 ---
Nests are made of twigs, grass, and other vegetation.

--- SENTENCE 1300 ---
Breeding is fairly synchronous but occurs throughout the year and timing varies by locality (Schreiber et al. 1996, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1301 ---
Several color phases exist, ranging from all brown to all white (Schreiber et al. 1996, Nelson 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1302 ---
The most common color morph at Rose is the intermediate form.

--- SENTENCE 1303 ---
They are monogamous and generally retain their mates throughout subsequent breeding seasons (Schreiber et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1304 ---
They lay 1 egg and continue to feed the young 1–2 months after fledging (Schreiber et al. 1996, Carboneras 1992).

--- SENTENCE 1305 ---
Sexual maturity begins around 3–4 years and most birds return to their natal colony to breed (Schreiber et al. 1996, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1306 ---
Adults usually breed every year but sometimes take a "rest" year (Schreiber et al. 1996, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1307 ---
Red-footed boobies feed on flying fish, squid, mackerel scads, saury, and anchovies (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1308 ---
Red-footed boobies often depart the colony to feed well before daylight and most return to the colony to roost at night (Carboneras 1992, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1309 ---
Red-footed boobies feed by plunge-diving and may feed solitarily or in mixed-species foraging flocks (Au and Pitman 1986).

--- SENTENCE 1310 ---
They forage further from land than other boobies except possibly the masked booby (Nelson 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1311 ---
Annual adult survival was estimated at 90% in a 2-year study at French Frigate Shoals in the NWHI (Hu 1991).

--- SENTENCE 1312 ---
At Johnston Atoll, survival of chicks to breeding ranged from 27 to 52% depending on the year (Schreiber et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1313 ---
The oldest-known bird was 22 years (Clapp et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1314 ---
The large areas of mangrove forests destroyed in American Samoa may have once been important habitat for this species.

--- SENTENCE 1315 ---
Introduced scale insects and other factors at Rose Island are destroying the *Pisonia* forest.

--- SENTENCE 1316 ---
Human predation on adults, chicks, and eggs may occur in parts of American Samoa (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1317 ---
El Niño-Southern Oscillation conditions can cause total or partial breeding failure in some locations (Schreiber and Schreiber 1989, Schreiber 1994).

### **4.5.7 Gogo Uli (***Anous minutus***) or Black Noddy**

!

--- SENTENCE 1318 ---
[](_page_88_Picture_6.jpeg)

*Nesting gogo uli.*

--- SENTENCE 1319 ---
USFWS

The gogo uli is an abundant and gregarious, medium-sized bird with a pantropical distribution (Gauger 1999, Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1320 ---
Adults are sooty black with a white cap on the top of the head.

--- SENTENCE 1321 ---
There are seven recognized subspecies and at least three breed in the USPI: *A. m. melanogenys* in the main Hawaiian Islands; *A. m. marcusi* in the NWHI, Wake, and throughout Micronesia; and *A. m. minutus* in Samoa (Gauger 1999, Gochfeld and Burger 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1322 ---
Breeding adults are mostly sedentary remaining at colonies year-round and foraging within approximately 50 miles of nesting islands

(Gauger 1999, Ashmole and Ashmole 1967, King 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1323 ---
Juveniles probably remain at breeding colonies or travel to nearby roosting sites (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1324 ---
The world population is estimated to be 1,000,000–1,500,000 pairs (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1325 ---
In the USPI, there are approximately 22,400 pairs.

--- SENTENCE 1326 ---
An estimated 12,000 pairs nest in the Hawaiian Islands, and smaller colonies exist in American Samoa, Palmyra, Johnston, and Wake Atolls, and the Marianas.

--- SENTENCE 1327 ---
Approximately 750 pairs use Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1328 ---
Worldwide population trends are unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1329 ---
The gogo uli nest on oceanic and offshore islands (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1330 ---
They place their nests on trees and bushes (Howard and Moore 1984, Harrison 1990); the nests on Rose Island are in *Tournefortia*  branches.

--- SENTENCE 1331 ---
Breeding is asynchronous and aseasonal.

--- SENTENCE 1332 ---
Birds are monogamous, mate retention is high, and pairs retain their territory from year to year, often reusing the same nest (Gauger 1999, Schreiber and Ashmole 1970).

--- SENTENCE 1333 ---
The gogo uli are capable of producing more than one brood per year and some lay a second egg while still tending the first chick (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1334 ---
Sexual maturity begins around 2–3 years (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1335 ---
The oldest-known bird was 25 years (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1336 ---
Black noddies feed by hover-dipping and contact-dipping, and typically forage in multi-species flocks over schools of predatory fish, especially tunas and jacks (Ashmole and Ashmole 1967).

--- SENTENCE 1337 ---
They feed mainly inshore (<6 miles from shore) and sometimes within several feet of the shoreline (Harrison 1990, Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1338 ---
Black noddies eat fish almost exclusively and very small amounts of squid and crustaceans (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1339 ---
In the central Pacific, flying fish, blennies, mackerel, and anchovies are important components of the diet (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1340 ---
Predation by introduced mammals in the breeding colonies limits populations and depletion of large predatory fish density due to fishing may reduce feeding opportunities (Gauger 1999).

--- SENTENCE 1341 ---
# **4.5.8 Gogo (***Anous stolidus***) or Brown Noddy**

The brown noddy is a medium-sized tern with a pantropical distribution (Chardine and Morris 1996), dark brown in color all over except for the whitish-gray cap on the top of its head.

--- SENTENCE 1342 ---
There are five subspecies; *A. s. pileatus* breed in the central and western Pacific (Harrison and Stoneburner 1981).

--- SENTENCE 1343 ---
Brown noddies have been shown to breed more than once per year in the NWHI (Megyesi and Griffin 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1344 ---
Breeding adults remain within sight of the colony, foraging in waters several tens-ofmiles from the colony (Morris and Chardine 1992, Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1345 ---
During nonbreeding periods, brown noddy have been shown to stay within 62 miles of colonies (Clapp et al. 1983, Harrison 1990)

or to migrate out of the area for several months (Murphy 1936, Morris and Chardine 1992).

--- SENTENCE 1346 ---
Little is known of the movements of juveniles (Chardine and Morris 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1347 ---
The world population is estimated at 500,000–1,000,000 pairs (Chardine and Morris 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1348 ---
Within the USPI, there are about 135,000 pairs (Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1349 ---
Approximately 9,000–11,000 pairs nest in American Samoa, the Marianas, and Johnston Atoll (Amerson et al. 1982, Reichel 1991).

--- SENTENCE 1350 ---
Approximately 200 pairs nest at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1351 ---
The population trend is probably

!

--- SENTENCE 1352 ---
USFWS

stable, but increasing in areas where predators were removed (e.g., Midway, Kure) (Chardine and Morris 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1353 ---
Brown noddies usually nest in loose groups or colonies and are flexible in nesting behavior.

--- SENTENCE 1354 ---
Nests are on the ground, often on open slopes or under vegetation but the brown noddy also nest on cliffs and in trees, especially where introduced mammalian predators are present (Harrison 1990, USFWS 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1355 ---
Brown noddy pairs stay together throughout the year, but there is little information on mate retention in subsequent years (Chardine and Morris 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1356 ---
Sexual maturity begins around 3–7 years and it is unknown whether birds return to their natal colony to breed (Chardine and Morris 1996, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1357 ---
The oldest-known bird was 25 years (Chardine and Morris 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1358 ---
Brown noddies feed by hover and contact-dipping in nearshore and off-shore waters (Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1359 ---
They often feed in association with tuna schools and can be found in mixed-species feeding flocks.

--- SENTENCE 1360 ---
The greatest threat is introduced predators, and where there are predators, brown noddy often nest in trees (Chardine and Morris 1996, Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1361 ---
Predation by introduced mammals, such as the Polynesian rat, has contributed to the extirpation of brown noddy from islands where they formerly nested (e.g., Lehua) (VanderWerf et al. 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1362 ---
Disturbance of the colonies can lead to increased predation by native predators: unprotected eggs are taken by atafa and shorebirds, especially when adults are flushed from nests by human disturbance.

### **4.5.9 Manu Sina (***Gygis alba***) or White Tern**

!

--- SENTENCE 1363 ---
*Nesting manu sina with egg on* Tournefortia *branch.

--- SENTENCE 1364 ---
The manu sina is small and entirely white, with a pantropical distribution (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, Gochfeld and Burger 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1365 ---
The manu sina has adapted well to humanaltered landscapes better than many other seabirds.

--- SENTENCE 1366 ---
It is perhaps the most familiar bird in Samoa (Craig 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1367 ---
There are four subspecies; *G. a. alba* breed in the central and western Pacific (Gochfeld and Burger 1996, Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1368 ---
Breeding adults remain close to colonies, foraging primarily inshore in shoals and banks but sometimes in offshore waters (Niethammer and Patrick 1998).

--- SENTENCE 1369 ---
During nonbreeding periods they disperse

from breeding grounds to sea but their range is unknown (Niethammer and Patrick 1998).

--- SENTENCE 1370 ---
Some adults are year-round residents on the colony (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1371 ---
Little is known of the movements of immature manu sina.

--- SENTENCE 1372 ---
World population is unknown but probably exceeds 100,000 pairs (Gochfeld and Burger 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1373 ---
In the USPI, there are about 17,000 pairs.

--- SENTENCE 1374 ---
Large colonies exist in American Samoa (3,900 pairs) (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1375 ---
Rose Atoll supports at least 60 pairs.

--- SENTENCE 1376 ---
World and USPI population trends are unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1377 ---
Manu sina nest on volcanic pinnacles, cliffs, rocky slopes, in large bushes or trees, or on artificial substrates (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, Rauzon and Kenyon 1984).

--- SENTENCE 1378 ---
They do not build nests but lay a single egg on a suitable depression, sometimes precariously balancing on small tree branches.

--- SENTENCE 1379 ---
Manu sina are monomorphic and monogamous, and partners remain together for several seasons, often returning to the same nest site (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1380 ---
Clutch size is one egg and some breeding pairs may successfully raise two or even three broods within a nesting season (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, VanderWerf 2003, Miles 1985).

--- SENTENCE 1381 ---
Manu sina feed primarily by dipping- and surface-diving (Niethammer and Patrick 1998).

--- SENTENCE 1382 ---
They often occur in mixed feeding flocks and usually in association with predatory fish (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1383 ---
Prey items include juvenile goatfish, flying fish, squid, needlefishes, halfbeaks, dolphinfishes, and blennies (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1384 ---
Although manu sina exhibit lower vulnerability to introduced predators than most seabirds because of their ability to use inaccessible (e.g., trees and sheer cliffs) nesting sites, introduced predators such as rats and cats have been the primary factor affecting populations (Niethammer and Patrick 1998).

--- SENTENCE 1385 ---
Scale insects have been introduced to Kure, Rose, and Palmyra Atolls where they attack native vegetation and reduce the number of nest sites in the native forest; the effects on manu sina nesting populations are not known.

--- SENTENCE 1386 ---
Depletion from fishing of large predatory fish stocks that drive prey to the surface may reduce foraging opportunities for manu sina (Niethammer and Patrick 1998, Gochfeld and Burger 1996).

### **4.5.10 Gogosina (***Onychoprion fuscatus***) or Sooty Tern**

Sooty terns have a pantropical distribution (Gochfeld and Burger 1996, Clements 2000, Schreiber et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1387 ---
There are eight subspecies; *O. f. oahuensis* breed in the central and south Pacific (Gochfeld and Burger 1996, Clements 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1388 ---
Breeding adults remain relatively close to colonies and forage up to 311 miles from breeding islands (Flint 1991, Gould 1974).

--- SENTENCE 1389 ---
During nonbreeding periods, they are highly pelagic and tend to avoid regions with cold-water upwelling (Gochfeld and Burger 1996, Schreiber et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1390 ---
Juveniles disperse widely after fledging and remain at sea, sometimes not touching land for several years (Schreiber et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1391 ---
The world population is estimated to range from 60 to 80 million pairs with 18–23 million pairs breeding each year (Schreiber et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1392 ---
In the USPI, there are approximately 3.2 million pairs.

--- SENTENCE 1393 ---
A large colony of more than 100,000 pairs breeds at Rose Atoll (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1394 ---
Sooty tern nest on oceanic islands and atolls in large dense colonies (Gochfeld and Burger 1996, Schreiber et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1395 ---
A colony usually consists of several subcolonies and each subcolony breeds very synchronously.

--- SENTENCE 1396 ---
Sooty tern nest on the ground in sandy substrate with sparse vegetation (Schreiber et

al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1397 ---
On Rose Island sooty terns also move into the forest and lay eggs in the open understory there.

--- SENTENCE 1398 ---
Sexual maturity begins around age 4–10 years (Schreiber et al. 2002, Harrington 1974).

--- SENTENCE 1399 ---
The oldest-known bird was 32 years (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1400 ---
Sooty terns, the most pelagic of the tropical terns (King 1967), feed mainly by aerial-dipping, contactdipping, and aerial capture, although they will plunge-dive (Gochfeld and Burger 1996, Schreiber et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1401 ---
Sooty terns tend to feed in large flocks with other species in association with predatory fishes, such as yellowfin and skipjack tunas

!

--- SENTENCE 1402 ---
Jiny Kim/USFWS

(Schreiber et al. 2002, Harrison 1990, USFWS 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1403 ---
El-Niño-Southern Oscillation conditions can cause breeding failure in the Pacific (Schreiber and Schreiber 1989).

--- SENTENCE 1404 ---
Native predators such as atafa and tuli take chicks and eggs (Schreiber et al. 2002, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1405 ---
Sooty terns are vulnerable to oil pollution from tankers and spills.

--- SENTENCE 1406 ---
Depletion of tuna by fisheries could potentially have an impact on the availability of prey (Schreiber et al. 2002).

### **4.5.11 Gogosina (***Onychoprion lunatus***) or Gray-backed Tern**

Gray-backed terns are endemic to the tropical and subtropical Pacific but are most common in the Central Pacific (Mostello et al. 2000, Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1407 ---
Breeding adults are mostly sedentary and forage up to 230 miles from land (Harrison 1990, Dixon and Starrett 1952).

--- SENTENCE 1408 ---
During nonbreeding periods, they are highly pelagic and occur far from breeding colonies, but their range is unknown (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1409 ---
At sea, gray-backed terns are found in highly saline waters (Ainley and Boekelheide 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1410 ---
There are limited data on movements, but juveniles travel great distances after leaving the natal colony (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1411 ---
The world population size is unknown but possibly on the order of 70,000 pairs (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1412 ---
Lack of adequate information on breeding phenology in many areas complicates estimates (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1413 ---
In the USPI there are approximately 48,000 pairs and 30 pairs nesting on Sand Island at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1414 ---
The global population trend is difficult to assess, but probably has declined since some colonies have been extirpated (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1415 ---
In the USPI, the population appears stable or increasing, but historical declines occurred at remote Pacific islands due to introduced predators.

--- SENTENCE 1416 ---
Trends in the USPI may be increasing with the removal of predators such as cats from many islands and places such as Howland, Jarvis, and Wake Atoll (Rauzon et al. 2011).

--- SENTENCE 1417 ---
Gray-backed terns breed on remote islands and atolls, on rocky ledges or sandy beaches often along vegetated edges bordering open areas (Amerson 1971, Ely and Clapp 1973).

--- SENTENCE 1418 ---
Their nests are shallow depressions in sand or gravel.

--- SENTENCE 1419 ---
Breeding occurs throughout the year.

--- SENTENCE 1420 ---
The clutch is one egg and chicks are semi-precocial when hatched (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1421 ---
Fledglings may remain at the colony up to 6 weeks after first flight (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1422 ---
The oldest-known gray-backed tern was 25 years (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1423 ---
Gray-backed terns feed mainly by plunge-diving or contact/hover-dipping.

--- SENTENCE 1424 ---
They are described as an inshore, offshore, or pelagic feeder due to the geographical and seasonal differences in foraging habitat (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1425 ---
Gray-backed terns eat five-horned cowfish, juvenile flying fish, goatfish, herring, dolphinfish, squid, crustaceans, mollusks, and marine and terrestrial insects (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1426 ---
Gray-backed terns can be found foraging in mixed-species flocks, especially with sooty terns and sometimes with ta'i'o (Gould 1971).

--- SENTENCE 1427 ---
In the USPI, their gravest threat is predation by introduced mammals such as rats and cats (Harrison 1990, Woodward 1972, Harrison et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1428 ---
They are sensitive to disturbance, leaving their eggs when humans approach (Harrison 1990).

--- SENTENCE 1429 ---
Unattended eggs and chicks are vulnerable to predators such as atafa and ruddy turnstones and curlews (Mostello et al. 2000).

--- SENTENCE 1430 ---
Gray-backed terns tend to nest near the surf zone and nests are often lost to storm tides (Mostello et al. 2000, Harrison 1990).

### **4.5.12 Gogosina (***Sterna sumatrana***) or Black-naped Tern**

!

--- SENTENCE 1431 ---
*Gogosina (black-naped tern) in flight.

--- SENTENCE 1432 ---
The black-naped tern is a white, small-sized bird with grayish-white back and wings and black beak and legs.

--- SENTENCE 1433 ---
This species has only recently (2010) been observed at Sand Island when a single adult individual was seen acting as if it might have a nest territory.

--- SENTENCE 1434 ---
No egg or chick was found.

--- SENTENCE 1435 ---
They breed on tropical and subtropical islands throughout the Indian and western Pacific Oceans.

--- SENTENCE 1436 ---
Breeding takes place on small offshore islands, reeds, sand spits, and rocky cays (Bird Life International 2011).

--- SENTENCE 1437 ---
Breeding season depends on locality (Bird Life International 2011) but have been recorded at breeding stations throughout the year, suggesting mainly sedentary habits (Harrison 1985).

--- SENTENCE 1438 ---
Colonies of 5–20 pairs are

formed, but sometimes up to 200 pairs can be formed (Bird Life International 2011).

--- SENTENCE 1439 ---
Colonies tend to be linear, or parallel to the water's edge, (Hulsman and Smith 1988) in the sand or gravel pockets on coral banks close to the high tide line and monospecific (del Hoyo et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1440 ---
They are also known to form colonies on shipwrecks (Hulsman and Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 1441 ---
One to two eggs, but occasionally three, are laid in either a shallow scrape on open ground or no nest is made (Hulsman and Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 1442 ---
Hulsman and Smith (1988) found that pebbles and small debris were thrown up toward the nest, having the effect of building up the nest edge, during nesting relief ceremonies.

--- SENTENCE 1443 ---
Black-naped terns hunt singly or in loose groups (Hulsman 1979) in atoll lagoons and nearshore, but they occasionally join flocks of black noddies when predatory fish are active near the reef (Hulsman and Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 1444 ---
Black-naped terns feed predominantly by plunging or air diving directly onto prey (Hulsman and Smith 1988, Bird Life International 2011), but become only semi-submerged (Harrison 1985).

--- SENTENCE 1445 ---
Both parents feed their young and make frequent flights to hunting grounds and young.

--- SENTENCE 1446 ---
Hulsman (1979) found anchovy to be a main food source for adults, but adults also consumed flying fish, mullet, barracuda, trevally or jack, tuna, damselfish, sardines, dolphinfish, grubfish, goby, blennies, and wrasse.

--- SENTENCE 1447 ---
Chicks were fed principally on the silver schooling fish belonging to the hardyheads and sprats, anchovies, and garfish.

--- SENTENCE 1448 ---
Black-naped terns are sensitive to human disturbance, either in terms of reduced breeding success or colony desertion.

--- SENTENCE 1449 ---
Black-naped terns nest in the open, which exposes their eggs and young to the weather.

--- SENTENCE 1450 ---
Adults must, therefore, shelter their eggs and chicks from the wide range of weather conditions experienced in tropical and sub-tropical areas.

--- SENTENCE 1451 ---
On two islands in Australia, the major causes of mortality of eggs and chicks were predation by gulls and flooding of nesting areas (Hulsman and Smith 1988), indicating that any introduced predators or excessive human disturbance would cause birds to flush, rendering chicks vulnerable to nonnative predators as well as native birds like tuli or atafa.

--- SENTENCE 1452 ---
# **4.6 Shorebirds and Wading Birds**

The Pacific Island Region functions as an essential migratory habitat for maintaining global shorebird populations.

--- SENTENCE 1453 ---
Rose Atoll is an important wintering ground for shorebirds in the Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 1454 ---
Seven species have been recorded at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1455 ---
The most common migratory shorebirds are the Pacific golden plover, ruddy turnstone, and wandering tattler.

--- SENTENCE 1456 ---
Some shorebirds primarily use the beach strand habitat; however, the littoral forest also serves as important habitat.

--- SENTENCE 1457 ---
The Pacific golden plover is the most abundant of the shorebird species in American Samoa (Engilis and Naughton 2004) and also the species that has been seen in largest numbers at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1458 ---
Information on the status, trends, and ecology of shorebirds in the Pacific and their use of Rose Atoll is lacking in published literature (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1459 ---
Information needs include assessment of population sizes and trends; assessment of the timing and abundance of birds at key wintering and migration stopover sites; assessment of habitat use and requirements at wintering and migration areas; exploration of the geographic linkages between wintering, stopover and breeding areas; and evaluation of habitat restoration and management techniques to meet the needs of resident and migratory species (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1460 ---
Many shorebirds wintering in the Pacific migrate over 2,486–7,458 miles of open ocean.

--- SENTENCE 1461 ---
Based on banding recoveries, patterns of distribution, and species assemblages, the following three flyways have been proposed: Asiatic-Palauan Flyway (birds move from Asia to Western Pacific and Philippine Sea Islands), Japanese-Mariana Flyway (mostly Asian birds move through Japan into the Mariana Islands and Caroline Islands), Nearctic-Hawaiian Flyway (birds breeding in Alaska and Eastern Siberia

--- SENTENCE 1462 ---
[Beringia] move through Hawai'i to Marshalls and Polynesia)

--- SENTENCE 1463 ---
The Service developed the USPI Regional Shorebird Conservation Plan (Engilis and Naughton 2004) over concerns of declining shorebird populations and loss of habitat.

--- SENTENCE 1464 ---
Threats to shorebirds in the Pacific region include loss of habitat, nonnative plants, nonnative animals (predation, disease, and competition), human disturbance, and environmental contaminants.

--- SENTENCE 1465 ---
Conservation and restoration of shorebird habitats in the USPI is a growing effort and essential for the protection of endangered and declining shorebird populations.

--- SENTENCE 1466 ---
Wetlands, beach strand, coastal forests, and mangrove habitats are particularly vulnerable on Pacific islands due to increasing development pressures and limited acreage.

--- SENTENCE 1467 ---
Shorebirds and Wading Birds of Primary Conservation Importance in the U.S. Pacific Region** 

| Species                | Regional Trend | Conservation category |
|------------------------|----------------|-----------------------|
| Pacific golden plover  | Unknown        | High concern          |

--- SENTENCE 1470 ---
### **4.6.1 Tuli (***Arenaria interpres***) or Ruddy Turnstone**

The ruddy turnstone is a common shorebird throughout the Pacific Islands; however, it is recognized as a species of Low Concern (Engilis and Naughton 2004) because the vast majority of its world population uses other areas for wintering grounds.

--- SENTENCE 1471 ---
Remote sandy islands appear to support the largest numbers of turnstones in the USPI, but there are no available survey estimates for the wintering population at American Samoa (Engilis and Naughton 2004).

--- SENTENCE 1472 ---
The largest group ever recorded at Rose Atoll was 45 in 1982.

--- SENTENCE 1473 ---
Ruddy turnstones use sandy and rocky beaches, reefs, and mudflats.

--- SENTENCE 1474 ---
### **4.6.2 Tuli (***Calidris alba***) or Sanderling**

The sanderling is widespread and locally common throughout the Pacific Islands.

--- SENTENCE 1475 ---
In the USPI, the sanderling is less often seen than wandering tattlers and tuli.

--- SENTENCE 1476 ---
The USPI Regional Shorebird Conservation Plan (Engilis and Naughton 2004) designated this shorebird as a species of limited importance in the Pacific Islands since the vast majority of sanderlings overwinter in other regions of the world.

--- SENTENCE 1477 ---
They are usually found on the water's edge in small groups where they run back and forth from the waves to feed on the small invertebrates exposed by the retreating waves.

### **4.6.3 Tuli (***Tringa incana***) or Wandering Tattler**

The wandering tattler is nowhere common but is ubiquitous throughout the Pacific region.

--- SENTENCE 1478 ---
Predominantly nearctic breeders, wandering tattlers migrate from their breeding grounds in Alaska and northwest Canada (Gill et al. 2002) to islands throughout the Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 1479 ---
During winter, they are solitary or occur in small groups of two to three birds throughout the Pacific Basin (Gill et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1480 ---
They are most common on rocky beaches but they also use a wide range of habitats including exposed reefs, sandy beaches, and mudflats (Engilis and Naughton 2004, Gill et al. 2002).

--- SENTENCE 1481 ---
The USPI Regional Shorebird Conservation Plan (Engilis and Naughton 2004) estimated the total population of wandering tattlers between 10,000 and 25,000 individuals.

--- SENTENCE 1482 ---
There are an estimated 900 wandering tattlers wintering in American Samoa (Amerson et al. 1982).

--- SENTENCE 1483 ---
*4.6.4 Matu'u (***Egretta sacra***) or Pacific Reef Heron**

The matu'u is a common bird in Samoa, with long legs and a long neck that is often curved in an Sshape.

--- SENTENCE 1484 ---
There are three color morphs: dark gray, pure white, or a combination of both colors in patches, and all have been observed at Rose Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1485 ---
The herons forage across the reef crest for a wide variety of reef fish, crabs, and snails, as well as freshwater streams for food.

--- SENTENCE 1486 ---
Matu'u construct their large nests in trees that are safe from predators.

--- SENTENCE 1487 ---
At Rose Island nests have been found in niu and *Cordia* surrounded by thick ferns (*Nephrolepis hirsutula*).

--- SENTENCE 1488 ---
In the 2010 field visit to Rose Atoll, there were two nests, one with two chicks and one with one chick.

--- SENTENCE 1489 ---
The white and dark color morphs were both seen on this visit.

--- SENTENCE 1490 ---
Population numbers in American Samoa are not known.

--- SENTENCE 1491 ---
# **4.7 Land Birds**

Rose serves as nonbreeding habitat for one austral migrant, the long-tailed cuckoo or aleva (*Eudynamis taitensis*).

--- SENTENCE 1492 ---
Vagrant birds are those that occasionally are blown off course by storms or by faulty directional decision during migration.

--- SENTENCE 1493 ---
Three vagrant species have been sighted at Rose Atoll: the cattle egret (*Bubulcus ibis*), snowy egret (*Egretta thula*), and the wattled honeyeater (*Foulehaio carunculata*).

--- SENTENCE 1494 ---
### **4.7.1 Aleva (***Eudynamis taitensis***) or Long-tailed Cuckoo**

The aleva migrates from New Zealand in the winter and forages toward the southwest Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 1495 ---
The center of its winter range lies in central Polynesia (Kepler et al. 1994).

--- SENTENCE 1496 ---
On Rose Island, its habitat is in dense and thick cover of the littoral forest.

--- SENTENCE 1497 ---
Single birds have been sighted 1976, 1980, 1990, and 1992.

--- SENTENCE 1498 ---
Two were observed in 1984.

--- SENTENCE 1499 ---
The very cryptic and stealthy behavior of this species makes it likely that it is more common than field observations would indicate and on some visits the bird is heard but not seen as in 2010.
